speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the two minute introduction to my comments in respect of this bill last evening I stated that after following very closely the statements made by the Registrar General during the resolution and second reading stages, and after reading the bill itself, I found myself somewhat troubled. I also said last evening that the presentation by the minister reminded me of something which I thought was a good expression of my opinion of his presentation and the bill. I further said that when this debate was resumed I would state exactly what the minister's presentation brought to mind.
Mr. Speaker, not too often but sometimes I watch television. On occasion when
3318	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs I do watch T.V. I see a spectacular called wrestling. In this spectacular called wrestling there appear two magnificently built brutes, cavemen, one of whom normally is accepted as being the good guy and the other as the bad guy. For a few moments they look at each other; then they grapple; then they go down, one under the other. They grunt and they groan, they scream and they sweat, but I have always noticed that the man underneath usually has one free arm so he can pound the canvas so the spectators will know the agony he is going through. You know, if I may use the expression of a person whose name I believe is Ed Sullivan, it is a "wonderful shew"-yes, a wonderful show.
I have read a great deal about these wrestling matches on T.V. I have spoken to some of the contestants. They all have to have a knowledge of wrestling fundamentals but they told me that the major fundamental is acting, putting on a show. Well, the wrestling on T.V. came to my mind with the presentation that was made by the minister and the reading of his bill. He put on a wonderful show, sir.
During his speeches at the resolution stage and on second reading the minister got up with all his eloquent words and grappled and sparred as a good guy with the bad guy. He talked about fighting the high cost of living and solving the problems of the consumer, and he referred to what the government intends to do. Then all of a sudden he reverted from a good wrestler to a character from Mother Goose. He stuck in his thumb and he pulled out a plum-Bill C-161-and said "What a good guy am I". The only problem is that the plum seems to be a little bit rotten.
This performance was like a wrestling match on television. It was all a sham and a joke. It was all hypothetical, because the minister did not grapple with these problems and has not included in his bill anything of a serious nature to deal with the high cost of living or to protect the consumer. They were well spoken words but represented nothing but wishful thinking.
Following this hypothetical groaning and straining the minister apologized for his lack of a solution to the problems and blamed this on the existence of jurisdictional and constitutional difficulties. He said the people would not accept controls and that there would be no price review board. I have been intrigued by the extent of the

DEBATES	October 20, 1967
government's militant and aggressive strategy and policies to win a shooting war, but how extraordinarily timid and hesitant they are in respect of policies, attitudes and actions for a war against poverty. Let me suggest that there is a war against poverty to be fought, because to protect consumers the government must restrain outrageous prices and exorbitant profits. This action is definitely part and parcel of a war on poverty.
In relation to the proposed legislation, we find nothing but wishful thinking and eloquent words expressed by the minister. When we find little or no specific attack on the problems of the consumer then I suggest this has been nothing but window dressing. When speaking on behalf of the government the minister referred to constitutional and jurisdictional problems and suggested the people would not accept controls. In view of the emergency I wander whether the people would accept controls. There is an emergency, in that we have inflation and spiralling costs of living. A great many of our people today can not exist with the present cost of living because of the low incomes they earn. Those on fixed incomes find it extremely difficult to even exist at this time.
Perhaps these people will not accept controls, but I wonder what their reaction might be if this government had the intestinal fortitude to say there is a crisis and there must be controls or they would not introduce this bill, and that they are prepared not just to control wages but also prices, profits, profit reserves and their use. If we intend to win this war against poverty and meet the economic crisis we now face militant action will have to be taken. If the government adopted this attitude and made that fact clear to the people, they might find a different reaction in respect of the acceptance of controls.
We have listened very carefully to the Minister of Finance on numerous occasions asking other people to tighten their belts. There might be a different reaction on the part of the people if this government and this House of Commons made it clear that we meant what we said. Although the reduction would be infinitesimal in the over-all picture, how about reducing the stipend of the members of the House of Commons and the Senate? This would be an indication to the people that we believe something must be done about the crisis which exists. Let me hasten to add that I think members are
October 20, 1967

underpaid in view of their responsibilities. There are 265 members on this board of directors for the 20 million people we represent, and we must do something on their behalf. If we believe we are now facing an economic and financial crisis as a result of spiralling costs of living, then we are morally obligated to take immediate action and do some belt tightening ourselves. By doing so we might create a different reaction regarding the necessity of imposing controls.
It is obvious that such an approach is not acceptable by the government. Let us at least consider adopting the immediate measures outlined by the minister in Bill C-161. At least the bill contains provision for research and the dissemination of information. As far as I can decide the major principles are contained in clause 6, paragraphs (c)	(d). If this represents all
the government will do, the government should aggressively use the power thus provided to stop inflation and spiralling costs. It should also make known to every citizen of Canada just what the situation is and what it intends to do. I am convinced that even though the government may not want to act, if it will make known through ministerial releases in the press, on radio and on television just what is causing this high cost of living, this will have a beneficial influence.
Let me give four clear illustrations of what I have in mind. Under the powers contained in clause 6 the government through this department will be able to exert some pressures in respect of consumer commodities. Over the years every time there has been an increase in the price of flour there has been an increase in the price of bread. Generally speaking the increases in the price of flour have amounted to only a fraction of one cent per loaf, but every time such an increase has occurred the price of a loaf of bread has been increased by two cents.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
When these things happen, will the minister call for a justification of such increases? He has his research and information officers and he should make known to the people of Canada that this is an unjustifiable increase. I gather, on the basis of quite a few years' experience in dealing with the public, that perhaps public opinion will compel the manufacturers and the provincial and federal governments to act so as to prevent such unjustifiable increases.
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
What more can I say than has already been said about the high cost of drugs? I read the report of the committee. The government was aware of this situation and announced it would remove the 11 per cent sales tax at the wholesale level. It also said that on the basis of the research done by the committee and the report which followed it recognized that the drug manufacturers had the highest net profits of any manufacturers or other industries, that it was unjustifiable and that if the price of drugs was not reduced further action might be contemplated by the government.
I ask the minister who is to head this new department, is he prepared to do something about the high price of drugs? Is he prepared to instruct his information service to disclose what is taking place? Let me give you one illustration by relating a persona] experience. A few months ago unfortunately I suffered from neuritis in the right shoulder; at least it was finally diagnosed as neuritis. I received a prescription, which I took to the pharmacy. I happen to have known the pharmacist for many years. He looked at the prescription and said "Harold, I can fill it right now, but can you wait for four hours? I have new stocks coming up from the wholesalers. To fill that prescription now would cost you $11, but if you wait four hours I will give you the same medicine but with a different brand name for $8." This sort of thing must be exposed. Companies should be named and brands should be named, and an exposure must be made of this sort of rapacious profiteering at the expense of those in our country who are ill.
Will the minister go further and investigate some other factors which have a great effect on the spiralling increase in the cost of living? Will he look into the reports and financial statements of large corporations and note that almost without exception they base their profit percentage on the sales of that year and compare it with the sales of the previous year or years? Since when should profit be based on the sales return percentage and not on capital investment? If honesty prevailed and profit were based on capital there would be a fantastic reduction in the cost of living to all the people of this country.
Will the minister look into that and expose this practice through his information service? Will he do more than that and look into the growing number of corporations in Canada which split their shares? I
3320	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs can think of one company which over the years has split one share into four, four into 16, 16 into 32 and 32 into 64. They state that the reason for doing this is to make the shares more readily available to the people who want to invest. This is eye-wash, because if one examines this practice, when a $100 share is split into 4 shares at $25, the value of the $25 share goes up immediately it hits the market. Anyone who buys the share at the higher price wants to profit from its return on the stock market price, which is not a fundamental basis of return. If you add to that the fact that many corporate directors get their shares at far less than the market value and make not millions of dollars but hundreds of millions through stock market manipulations for which eventually the consumer has to pay, the unfairness is compounded.
If my hon. friend the minister is sincere he will use his ability, his knowledge and his capabilities to ensure that under the present Bill C-161 he will make a start in the war against poverty and will put a road block to further inflation and the increasing cost of living.
The answer does not rest in our hands on this side of the house. At the present time it does not even rest in the hands of the people of Canada. It rests in the hands of the government in general, and in particular on the intestinal fortitude of the minister who will head this department and be in charge of its policy and its administration.
What does this bill really mean? To the majority of the people of Canada it means that a policy of wait and see is being adopted by the government. I hope this period of wait and see will not be too long in duration. As I said last night, I might have to make an agonizing reappraisal of my hon. friend for whom I have had the utmost respect and admiration. I hope that in the administration of the new department he will exercise determination and utilize every power possible to protect the consumers, to stop the spiralling increase in the cost of living and perhaps even to reduce it.
I will draw my remarks to a close by saying that many hon. members who have spoken before me have perhaps somewhat embarrassed the minister by drawing to his attention the obvious fact that he is a young and handsome man. I will conclude by reminding the minister of an old and truthful saying, namely that handsome is as handsome does.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always delighted to follow the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). In some ways he has made my task easier, because he has painted in a colourful way some of the problems which confront us and which I am sure will confront the minister. However, I may have to disagree with some of the proposals he has made.
When the minister introduced the resolution, accompanied by the usual publicity which is given to a measure of this kind, it seemed to us that at long last we might have been receiving for the benefit of the consumer a giant, economy size package. But when we came to read the bill we found that far from being the package we had hoped it would be, it was only about half full and instead of soap it contained mostly apple sauce. I believe all members will agree that this government, indeed all governments, face a very difficult problem in connection with this aspect of consumer prices.
[DOT] (12 noon)
When members of parliament are asked to exercise their responsibilities as representatives of the people of Canada in connection with a particular bill they ask themselves, first of all, what evil is it seeking to cure or, alternatively, what benefits will be secured by the passage of the legislation? When we look at bills we often find there is a preamble which sets out the purposes and intentions of the legislation. In this bill we have the bald statement that it is an act to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs.
The corporate aspect can be set to one side because this is a matter over which this parliament has exercised jurisdiction for some time. The government has been invested with certain responsibilities in connection with corporate affairs which could be properly collected together and brought under one minister. I believe this is sound, common sense.
What do we mean by consumer affairs? There is really nothing in the bill to guide us, and from what I have heard of the debate thus far we can form one of two opinions of the government's intention. First, this bill may be intended to indicate that the government of Canada is going to make a real, meaningful attempt to come to grips with one of the most serious problems affecting not only this country but most countries in the western civilization, the escalation of prices of goods and services to a point where they
October 20, 1967	COMMONS
are beyond the capacity of many people to meet and provide a reasonable standard of living for their families. I do not believe there is any doubt about the fact that we have moved in the last two or three generations from a rural society into a complicated, basically urban society in which the machinery of production as well as the machinery of supply and demand have become increasingly complicated. I think many people today are discontented, unhappy, frustrated and becoming exceedingly angry at the fact there seems to be no real effort on the part of the mysterious "they", as governments are described today, to do anything about the situation.
I think we had an excellent example of this last year when there was a virtually spontaneous demonstration across this land by housewives and people whose task it is to go to the markets to buy the goods and services required by their families. I think the fact that the joint committee of this house and the other place, which was inquiring in a rather pedantic and pedestrian way into consumer credit, was suddenly seized with a great measure of anxiety about consumer affairs turned that committee into a more attractive and more meaningful body. It then secured authority to make an investigation into consumer prices.
When we talk about consumer affairs, at first blush there appears to be no doubt that most people think of consumer affairs in terms of the prices which consumers have to pay. This is one aspect of the matter with which I want to deal more extensively in a minute or two. On the other hand, consumer affairs may be regarded in a narrow, restricted way in relation to the constitutional rights and limitations which are placed upon this government in relation to the question of research and advice. If that is the intent of the government, then later I propose to say that we did not need this legislation. I propose to say that by means of taking advantage of existing legislation, existing regulations, with possibly a very minor amendment to the government organization measure, we would not have needed this bill at all.
I have come to the conclusion that the only basic purpose behind the passage of this legislation is to introduce into government organization the glamorous name of consumer affairs. This could well be a double-edged sword. I am not going to make the point that there is nothing that can be done if we follow either one of these directions in dealing with consumer affairs, either the broad 27053-210
DEBATES	3321
Corporate and Consumer Affairs measure of dealing with consumer prices or the restricted way of dealing with the problem through research. The bill refers to cooperation and co-ordination of government programs and undertakings or programs in co-operation with provincial governments. This is a narrow, restricted interpretation which can be placed on the intention of the government in setting up this department under a separate minister.
I should like to deal first with the question, can anything be done by the federal government within the limits of its constitutional and financial responsibilities? Point after point has been made by hon. members in this house that we must not follow the Procrustean method and, merely because the victim does not fit the bed, either stretch him or cut off his legs. This would be the course to follow if we adopted the philosophy of the Greek myth about the bed of Procrustes. I cannot agree with that. In my opinion, laws were made for the benefit of man and man does not exist for the purpose of being tortured, cribbed, cabined or confined within the limits of existing legislation.
This does not make our task any easier from the constitutional viewpoint. Unfortunately, we are entangled in the web of our own constitutional law-making. Whether we like it or not, the constitution exists until we devise some ways and means of changing it. We can, therefore, only do in this parliament what we are authorized to do by the British North America Act. It is all very well to say, let us do this, let us proceed on this particular scale to deal with this problem. In the present very sensitive stage of federal-provincial relations, I am sure any attempt to break out of these narrow limitations would be bound to be met not only by legal proceedings but by sound and very strong objections from provincial governments.
With this in mind, then, can anything be done? A reference was made earlier to conditions which existed during the war. To be honest, I do not really believe it is feasible to adopt the course followed during the war. I would object to it not only because it would be constitutionally wrong, but I feel it would be wrong in practice to set up in this country the tremendous organization required to oversee the prices and costs of goods and services. As a corollary, we would also have to oversee production. Surely there is no one in this country, certainly no one in this parliament, who would suggest that this problem needs to be tackled in that way. Such a course would set loose a Pandora's box of wrongs,
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs nuisances and evils far worse than those we are attempting to cure. I do not think anybody has argued that we in this country should at this stage do anything approximating what we were compelled to do during the war years.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) has from time to time rather persuasively brought up the proposal of a prices review board. This is a method which in a limited way was introduced into the United Kingdom, which of course is a unitary state with no constitutional problem. Perhaps there need be no constitutional problem here, Mr. Speaker, because balanced on the narrow edge of the criminal law it might be feasible to enjoin corporations and unions, in fact everyone who is engaged in the business of production and selling, to publish well in advance of the time when prices are to be increased evidence of their intention to do so.
We tend to think of this concept, Mr. Speaker, in terms of our own particular examination of the problem. I am sure there are some members in this house who could find some large and iniquitous corporations in this country to whom this sort of arrangement could be well applied. On the other hand, other hon. members would say that this approach should be taken toward labour unions because some labour unions have improperly importuned their employers at critical times, sometimes only for jurisdictional purposes, in order to secure wage increases which under the circumstances were not justified.
These two differing points of view may in themselves be quite correct. However, I would point out that if we attempt to solve the problem in this way we cannot stop just with the large corporations and the unions. We must institute the program in such a way that there is total involvement in the intricate make-up of our economic life. For example, every storekeeper who runs a corner store and wants to increase his prices and every employer who employs three or four persons would be caught up in the same web, and at this stage I do not think that this is a reasonable or a necessary means to deal with the problem. I just do not think it would work. I think that the cost of imposing a prices review board system would become appallingly high and would add to the problem of inflation now facing us. I do not think that this approach would be feasible. The enforcement machinery would be so large and expensive, so opposed to our concept of
[Mr. Baldwin.)

freedom to which we have adhered in this country for so many years.
Is there perhaps a third way, Mr. Speaker? I do not know. However, I would make this suggestion to the minister, though he might well have it in mind. Surely it might be possible in co-operation with the provinces to establish a joint board which, without being restricted to the criminal law alone, as is the case so far as the parliament of Canada is concerned, would have the jurisdiction to examine this issue. We all know very well that no government can delegate authority to another government; judicial decisions have held that to be so. However, it would be possible through the establishment of a tribunal which would be invested with some power by the federal parliament and with some authority by the provincial governments to examine glaring cases of abuse of our free enterprise system in the fixing of prices and the increasing of wages. In the kind of society in which we live I believe that the various public media would be quick to point out such abuses. If we could expose such cases to the broad glare of public opinion from time to time after suitable investigation had been made, then it might be possible to provide some kind of average test which others in the country could follow and which might be used in order to keep within reasonable restraint increases in prices, goods and services.
This would not be easy, Mr. Speaker. The options open to any government in any part of the world today are far more limited than they were 40 or 50 years ago. Sensitivities of one part of the world to another part, economic relations and rapid means of communication and transportation have brought this about. We in Canada particularly have found that our proximity to our great trading partner to the south, to whom we sell and from whom we buy large quantities of goods and services, has put us in such a position that no government has the degree of freedom it would need to deal with this problem properly in such a way as it might have been dealt with 40 or 50 years ago.
However, Mr. Speaker, there are some options open which have not been exercised. I want to emphasize that I am only putting forward this proposal for consideration by the minister, but I think there are means that can be used if there is a real desire on the part of the federal government and the provincial governments to deal with this matter. Let us bear in mind that these governments represent the people of Canada, and
October 20, 1967	COMMONS
the people in the province of Alberta and also the people in the province of Quebec are people of this country, people of Canada. I think it is high time that we should remove problems that have been created by a certain amount of jealousy between governments at the provincial level and the federal level. Our particular task here and the task of all legislators in all the provinces is to deal with those things and to engage in those measures that we think will enhance the interests of the people of the country at large.
There is then, Mr. Speaker, this possibility which might be looked at. However, before we could embark upon such a system the government of this country-perhaps also the governments of the provinces but certainly the federal government-would have to set its own house in order. How difficult it would be for the government of Canada to undertake to act responsibly in dealing in this way with prices and costs without first looking at its own area of expenditure.
I am not going to deal with this point extensively because we have been all through it during the budget debate and other members of the house have spoken about it. For example, we have been told that when the estimates come down we will be astounded at the extent to which the knife has been wielded. That is all very well, Mr. Speaker; when the estimates are available we will look at them. But bear in mind that more is involved than the estimates alone. When one looks at the estimates at the beginning of the year and then compares them with the actual expenditures made for that year which show up in the following year's estimates, hundreds of millions of dollars have been added by way of supplementary estimates at one time or another and this increases tremendously the money that is actually spent.
I suggest that this government cannot conscientiously ask industry or labour to show restraint with regard to increases in prices or wages until it is able to demonstrate beyond any reasonable doubt that it in turn has been prepared to set its own house in order. And this we are waiting to see. If it does happen I will be the first to give all credit to the government, and I hope that the minister will not take it amiss if I say that at the present time I am from Missouri so far as these proposed cuts are concerned.

speechtext:
Now let us look at the question from the more limited aspect of the proposals that are contained in this bill. These are pretty well set out in clause 6 and I am not going to deal with them too extensively. All they consist of is the right to undertake to co-ordinate programs of the government of Canada, which is what the Economic Council of Canada proposed. You do not need legislation for that; you do not need legislation to initiate, recommend or undertake programs designed to promote the interests of the Canadian consumer.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
One must bear in mind the wording of this legislation which says that the only matters over which the minister has responsibility are matters over which this parliament has jurisdiction and which are not by law assigned to any other department of government. The minister's right to initiate and recommend programs designed to promote the interests of the Canadian consumer is not a right which is given to him through this legislation. He has that right without the benefit of this legislation. His right to cooperate with provincial governments is a right which he has today; there is no question of that. His right to engage in research is a right which he has today. Apart from clause 1 which creates the department of corporate and consumer affairs, every power, every right and every responsibility which accrues to the minister through this bill could have been exercised under existing legislation. I could undertake to guide the minister through several statutes to show him exactly what I mean. The only reason for enacting this legislation is to create a department which, within its title, bears the words "consumer affairs". The legislation itself does not meet the needs of the people.
It may be remembered that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam yesterday referred to the poll that was conducted by Montreal Star. I looked at that report and from my reading of it, it indicates that only 31 per cent of those polled knew anything about the new department. Of that 31 per cent, approximately 70 per cent believed or
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs hoped that the minister and the new department would be concerned with prices. Perhaps the minister wishes to know how I arrived at my totals. I added the percentages of those who were interested in controlling profits and prices to the percentages of those who were concerned with a lower cost of living, and the result came to approximately 70 per cent of the original figure of 31 per cent. I expect the minister will accept my mathematics, unless he wants my figures to be research by the new department.
The minister, who is a member of the bar in several provinces and a businessman of some acumen, must have struggled with his political instincts, because I am sure he did not wish to leave a false impression. He must have recognized the grave limitations, legally and economically, of what could be done as a result of the creation of the new department.
I give the minister credit for his speeches. I am sure that his instincts as a politician led him to believe in the efficacy of the magic words "consumer affairs". No doubt he saw himself in the role of protector of the housewife when she enters a supermarket. She would walk hand in hand with him through the rows of goods and commodities and would feel safer knowing that "John Turner is looking after me."

speechtext:
As I say, though the minister spoke carefully I thought he allowed his instincts as a politician to prevail occasionally. If he is honest when he sums up before the bill receives second reading, he will admit that it does not invest the government with any new rights or authority and, that its authority already is limited economically and legally.
The only possible solution, as I suggested, would be that kind of collaboration with the provinces which would result in the institution of a joint board to which there could be delegated an adequate degree of authority, not with respect to the prices of all goods, commodities and labour across the country but with respect to pinpointing particularly glaring cases where the rights of the Canadian consumer have been ignored or where the Canadian consumer has been ruthlessly exploited. If this were done and a few instances were brought to light as examples, I think the benefit would be substantial.
As I said at the resolution stage, I regret that this bill did not go to a committee. I expect that the minister will say that the committee on consumer credit held hearings


all over the country and explored this entire question. He may say that, considering the number of witnesses it heard, to send this bill to a committee would be merely repetition. I do not think so. I have become increasingly convinced that there must be a better way of dealing with legislation than at present. The government conceives it in the darkest corners of its privy council closets and becomes attached to it by virtue of parenthood. It brings the legislation before the house and then refuses to accept amendments.
It seems to me that a bill designed to meet the present serious problems confronting the consumers of this country ought to have been sent to a committee before second reading. It is still not too late to do that. Great numbers of witnesses need not be called. There might be some sort of terms of reference and a limitation of time. Before that committee there could be presented the views of hon. members who sit to our left, of hon. members of the official opposition, as well as the views of others who are interested. In committee we could join issue on the problems we face. When the bill was returned to the house it would reflect the thinking of the members of the committee, who in turn are pipe lines of communication with their constituents, the consumers of Canada. I am not alone in thinking this.
During the debate in 1965 on the report of the procedure committee the following words were uttered, as found on page 12588 of Hansard:
It means we shall establish a procedure whereby legislation can be submitted at an earlier stage to standing and special committees of the commons for scrutiny by members. This reform would, in my opinion, achieve two main results. First, it would allow an individual member of parliament access to information upon which to base intelligent criticism.
I see the minister smiling. He will recognize the author of that statement. It was made before the minister ascended to the rarified atmosphere of the privy council. I will not say that he had more intelligence then than he has now. I will simply say that he occupied a lower position and had not attained the privilege of being a member of the privy council.

I think there would be unanimous approval of any technique that the minister or his associates could devise which would serve to control prices. Every one of us is concerned in one way or another about the high cost of living. It is certainly refreshing to hear the hon. member emphasize the extreme difficulties which would be involved in setting up machinery to control prices. By the same token it is disconcerting when other hon. members less objective in their approach do not recognize, or at least seem not to recognize, that the control of prices would involve far reaching and complex activities and that it simply could not be achieved without at the same time requiring, for example, the control of incomes and intervention in a host of other spheres related to this delicate and difficult subject.
Where I part company with the hon. member who spoke immediately before me is on his contention that the work which the new department is designed to perform could have been carried out without setting up the addition to the administrative machinery which the bill before us proposes. The minister himself has stated that there will be
Corporate and Consumer Affairs difficulties and shortcomings and that in the initial stages mistakes will probably be made. But it does seem to me that a focal point has now been created, a department which will have as its major responsibility the broad area of concern for consumers, and I do not believe that a variety of agencies could act as effectively.
I have had a fairly close association with various phases of marketing over the years and my native province has the questionable distinction of supporting the highest cost of living of any part of Canada. Many references have been made to the difficulties we in Newfoundland face because of a variety of circumstances which have resulted in costs that by mainland standards can only be described as fantastically high. Having lived in this atmosphere and having experienced these difficulties and noted, by the way, that along with the highest cost of living we also have the lowest per capita earnings of any part of Canada, I for one welcome any effort which is likely to bring these two factors into better balance.
The minister himself has said there must be consultation with the provinces. I heartily agree. I believe this is an approach which ought to be taken soon. Within a short time we shall be dealing with drug legislation, and we know that so much of the force which generates the high cost of drugs is within the control of the provinces and outside the control of the federal government. In this field, then, as well as in the whole field of consumer goods, consultation will be of the utmost importance.
It is impossible in the short time available to me to range over all the implications of this bill, so I should like to say a word about a subject which I believe is of greater importance than has been recognized by many of us up to the present time. There is, in my opinion, a great need for consumer education. A great deal has been said in the house about the high cost of living but I think it is fair to say too that at least within certain groups what we are suffering from is not so much the high cost of living as the cost of high living. This is a direction in which I believe education can accomplish much. There is nothing to prevent the new department launching a well-developed, well-thought-out program of consumer education.
I do not believe the department can do it alone. From my own experience I feel that there is a great need in our school system and in the whole of our educational process to lay more emphasis, when talking to young

Since the beginning of this debate, Mr. Speaker, I have listened to 15 or 16 speeches. I am one of those who believe that in spite of all the efforts of the minister, the cost of living will continue to rise. He may perhaps


halt the increases but not much. Then, monster delegations will descend upon him, loudly protesting and accusing him of all sorts of things such as was reported in the newspapers of the past few days about the chairman of a bank charging the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) with having misled the people and having practised a massive swindle. Such things will then be said to the minister who will have to fight the very people he wants to help. I do not say that to discourage him, because I know, of course, that he is brave and that he is ready to face the music; I mention it so that he and his associates may be realistic.
I would even like to remind him of something else. We have crisis here, there and everywhere and I infer from that that if we are experiencing so many crises-it is useless for me to enumerate them, because hon. members do so every day-it is because there is failure somewhere.
I have said it before and I say it again to strike the imagination of those I am referring to. I am not necessarily a Creditiste, I am not yet a socialist but I say nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the two old parties which are operating within a capitalistic system which is going out of fashion, within private enterprise which pleads and admits itself that we are faced with bankruptcy within a system which has failed to attain a fair distribution of the good things the Lord has provided for all Canadians-while a few are getting fat, others are deprived of bare necessities-within a capitalistic or free enterprise system which has failed to provide a fair distribution of the reasonable minimum of commodities without which according to St. Thomas Aquinas, a Roman Catholic theologian, a Christian cannot gain salvation, I say that now more than ever is the time to find a solution.
From day to day, what we hear in this house from all parties, is an avowal of the failure of the capitalistic, free enterprise system.
I will not say that the ideal solution necessarily lies with the creditist or socialist systems, but I say to both the old parties, which get funds from large capitalist interests who admit they have failed, while putting the blame on government representatives, though

consciences, because the public is beginning to grumble. The capitalists should meet, or at least those who hold the reins of our capitalist system; they should quit thinking that through concern or the handsomely paid propaganda of public relations men, they will have the people believe that they are not hungry when they are famished, that by dilly-dallying they will calm them down and silence them.
This era is over, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that if the minister wants to succeed, if he hopes to overcome the opposition, mainly, of the business circles who control the life blood of the country, he will have to coax the latter into self-examination until they understand they had better proceed on their own with a revision of the present system, and adapt to the conditions of 1967, or even of the forthcoming year 2000. Those are disturbing demonstrations and I believe that if the minister seeks to get at the root of the evil, he will have to tackle those things first of all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the bill now before us for second reading. Bill C-161 is designed to set up a department of corporate and consumer affairs. Every one of my constituents and every constituent whom other hon. members represent is a consumer, and I believe that all those who spoke here today were speaking in their interests and on their behalf. In order to voice their great concern over the increasing costs of consumer goods I wish to emphasize their demand that the government take definite and positive action with regard to rising prices. I say definite and positive action because, as other hon. members have said, we are not convinced that under Bill C-161 this will be done.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
We are all aware of the agitation of consumers during the last two years over rising prices. We have heard their insistent demands, as voiced through the Consumers Association of Canada. We have seen some of their demonstrations and have read some of their briefs to the government. I get the

impression now that at long last the government senses that the public is demanding more government involvement in this problem which affects every household in the country. Bill No. C-161 appears to be the government's answer. Does it meet the demands of the consumer or is it, as some hon. members have suggested, just window dressing? Is it an attempt to give the public a glamorous or important feeling and create the impression the consumer will have a voice in the councils of the mighty?
The minister who will be in charge of this new department is very friendly and charming. However, it will take more than charm, I am sure, to satisfy the consumers who have seen the purchasing power of their dollar eroded almost monthly. If I may be facetious for a moment, I should like to refer to the fact the bill says the minister will hold office at pleasure. Of course this means at the pleasure of the government. He will also have to look to the pleasure of the consumers in a large way. I feel he is going to have a very difficult job in this regard. I do not believe the provisions of the bill are sufficiently strong to allow him to satisfy the consumer.
I have a brief from the consumers association before me, but I shall not refer to it at any great length. It was presented by the Consumers Association of Canada in March, 1960, to the government. Several statements are contained in the brief to which I shall refer a little later relating to the concern of these people over prices. I also have a letter from the president of an organization called "Women Against Soaring Prices", which I imagine works closely with the Consumers Association of Canada.
This organization, Women Against Soaring Prices, asked for and I imagine received a hearing from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The letter reads in part:
Sir, we have a petition regarding this urgent subject-
Prices.
-signed by 12,000 ol our fellow citizens and addressed to you. We therefore respectfully request an appointment at your earliest convenience at which we can place that petition in your hands directly, and, we hope, discuss with you what can be done to combate soaring prices on essential foods and skyrocketing rentals.
I quote that part of the letter because while we have been referring quite often to soaring prices of foods, rentals certainly have been soaring as well. I think each one of us is acquainted with that fact, and it is part of the problems of the consumer as well. I put
Ociober 20, 1967

on the record earlier a letter from a senior citizen who, of necessity, must have drugs each day. She sent me a voucher she received dated April 6, 1967 for a drug costing $1.70. On April 25, about three weeks later, the same drug cost $2.90. The voucher for April 25 contained this notation:
There has been a price increase on this prescription in compliance with the new pricing schedule. Thank you.
This represents an increase of $1.20 on that drug. I believe increased drug prices will be a problem the minister's department will have to tackle too. Perhaps I should put on the record the figures relating to the repeated increases in the cost of living. The graph I have is headed:
What every housewife knows.
The advance of living costs was sharply faster in the past six months than it was in the same period during any of the previous three years.
The figures are taken from a Dominion Bureau of Statistics release. In 1964 the index rose from 134 to 137; in 1965, from 138 to 141; in 1966, from 142 to 146, and in the first half of 1967, from 146 to past 150. The graph certainly indicates a continual rise in the index, and this trend will continue unless the minister has more power than he would appear to have under this bill.
In the Saskatchewan Bulletin for October, 1967, we find a table setting out average family expenditure patterns for a family of four. In 1959 the exenditure on food amounted to $1,247, and in 1967 to $1,520. The expenditure on housing in 1959 amounted to $854, and in 1967 to $1,000. As has been pointed out by others, the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials is probably responsible for part of this increase. I will not quote all the items but they all show increases.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go back into history for a minute. I am referring to a time which the minister would perhaps not remember too well, namely, the period of the wartime prices and trade board. I am not advocating that we have price controls such as we had then because we had a war emergency at that time and we were all working in the national interest. However, I am sure the minister can obtain some useful information, if he has not already done so, by consulting the files of the wartime prices and trade board. He might even find some information in his family files because his family had a direct connection with this board, but I shall not refer to that now. I am just making this
Corporate and Consumer Affairs reference, for the information of the minister. There are details there of consumer education and consumer protection to which I shall refer later.
I should like to read part of an article which sets forth the objectives of the wartime prices and trade board. As I say, I am not advocating price controls such as existed at that time.
It makes all the difference to the happiness and
smooth running of a home if there is some semblance of economic stability. It makes it a lot easier for the housewife if she knows that the prices of staple foods like bread and milk and flour will be just about the same next month as they are today, if she has some assurance that the landlord won't jump the rent, and that the savings in the bank will buy just as much next year as they do right now.
This article was written in 1942, but I believe we should try to attain the same objectives today. May I refer very briefly to a short article about the minister and his proposed consumer department, and I do so to give him full warning of what is ahead of him. The minister stated that this department will concentrate on the dissemination of information and the educational aspects of consumer buying. It will primarily be a service department answering questions from consumers and businessmen. Correspondence followups will be one of the most important aspects of the new department.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
This is why I have referred in particular to the wartime prices and trade board. In the operation of that board there was a consumers branch which was under the jurisdiction of the former Byrne Hope Sanders. That branch was evidence of the fact that as women do 80 to 85 per cent of all buying of goods and services they are a very important part of the battle to keep down prices. What I wish to emphasize to the minister is that this consumers branch had a network across Canada and linked with every women's group, and at the end of 1944-I have the record here-the English and French officers of the branch numbered nearly 16,000. This indicates how women can organize. I suggest that if the minister plans on answering the letters of all these women he will certainly have a job on his hands in this department. In this connection I emphasize what others have said, namely, the danger of building up an empire of his own in a great bureaucracy.
I should like to quote an article on this point which appeared in last night's Ottawa
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs Journal. The heading reads "C.S. Jobs Increased By 1,000 Monthly In '66" and the opening paragraph is as follows:
Employment in the federal civil service grew last year at an average rate of better than 1,000 a month, a pace unmatched since the crash build-up during the second world war.
That was when the wartime prices and trade board was building up its personnel. The article goes on:
Civil service employment has been creeping up steadily from its wartime peak of 116,000 in 1945. But it didn't really start to surge until the start of 1965. Since then it has increased by an astonishing 9 per cent.
I hope that the minister does not have in mind the building up of an organization anything like that.
The brief of the Consumers Association of Canada stated that at present there is no focal point in the government for consumer policy, to focus attention on how policies affect consumers. I think this could be the most important place that the minister could occupy in the battle against rising prices. He will be meeting with his colleagues and it will be up to him-certainly we in the house have not been able to do it-to convince the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and construction machinery is increasing the price not only of homes but also of goods.
The minister will also have to convince the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) that the present rate of interest on mortgages of 8J per cent is adding to the cost of homes, which in turn adds to the problems of consumers. In addition he will have to convince the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), as we have tried to, that on many occasions the unfair application of the estate tax makes it necessary for small businesses to sell out in order to pay this tax, thus reducing competition and benefiting the large retail outlets.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, the minister will certainly have to convince the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), who I imagine will take a lot of convincing in view of his other performances in this house, as well as his former colleague, now head of the transport commission, that increases in freight rates add to the cost of consumer goods. Coming as 1 do from the west I refer especially to the removal of the bridge subsidy on the long haul north of the great lakes, which certainly adds to the cost of consumer goods.
I should now like to refer to a matter on which I have spoken previously. It is something for which the consumers themselves
[Mr. Pascoe.l

are to blame and perhaps the minister can persuade them otherwise. I refer to the expensive diet fads which are the trend now across the country. I speak on this subject with some interest because I am a wheat farmer. I suggest that the consumers of Canada get back to the good old nutritional habit of eating more bread. I do not agree with some statements that have been made to the effect that bread is not good for you. It certainly is; it is a very healthy food.
speakername: Mr, J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Cenire):

speechtext: I would certainly match those western housewives who bake their own bread against any women in eastern Canada who are on a diet. I think western housewives who eat bread will win the prize both for charm and beauty as well as health. I object to this trend not to eat bread. Today women are asked, yes, and men too, to eat imported grapefruit when we in the west have the wheat waiting to be turned into bread. Therefore if the minister could convince these people to return to the eating of bread he will have done his duty in this regard.

speechtext: Don't forget eating apples too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, an apple a day, but that will be hard on the doctors.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, I think a great deal of the experience gained by the wartime prices and trade board will help the minister. I realize we cannot impose the restrictions of those days such as price ceilings and rationing because the problem is different now. But many of the approaches of the board worked then and some of them will work now.
May I conclude by repeating what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said, namely, that before the bill was brought in the matter should have been referred to the standing committee where witnesses would have been able to present opinions. Had that been the case I think the government would have come up with a much better bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every observer of Canada and Canadians remarks on our diversity, diversity of region, of occupation, of religion, of language, even of politics, if I can mention that word in this august chamber. But among the things that we have in common is the fact that obviously we are all consumers.
October 20, 1967

It has already been pointed out at an earlier stage in this debate that the late President Kennedy, in his first message to the United States congress, said that consumers have rights, the right to be informed, the right to choose, the right to safety, the right to be heard. I think that this applies to Canada as well. The citizen as a consumer is entitled to ask that these rights be protected where necessary, by the organized community, by government, no less than the more traditional rights of free speech, religion and so on.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
There is a federal responsibility in this area of consumer interest and through this bill the government is attempting to have this federal responsibility carried out more actively and effectively than ever before. It would not be fair to the worker, to the family man concerned about how far his pay cheque will go, to give him the impression that the responsibility for consumer affairs can be carried out solely at the federal level. It is one which at present must be shared by the federal government with the provinces. But even under our existing constitutional arrangements there is a federal jurisdiction in consumer affairs which the federal government must use actively and creatively. Aside from a number of specific constitutional powers which have permitted it to act in the past in such areas as inspection of food and drugs to assure purity and safety, and in the area of weights and measures, the federal government in recent years has assumed a general obligation to keep the economy operating at a high level, which I think makes it necessary for it to take the consumer interest into account. This obligation involves efforts to maintain high levels of employment and income together with reasonable price stability.
Consumer expenditure on goods and services, according to the first report of the economic council, has been twice as large as all other uses of domestic output combined since the 1920's. In fact, 68 per cent of the gross national product in 1963 went for this type of expenditure. Twenty three per cent of family expenditures in Canada is for food. For low income families this figure rises to nearly 30 per cent, with another 40 per cent being taken for shelter, transportation and clothing.
Obviously, one key way of maintaining standards of living and making the pay cheque go farther is to make it possible for the consumer to make wise choices when he
Corporate and Consumer Affairs goes out to purchase, and to protect him from being misled and deceived in the marketplace. It must be clear by now that market forces, the pressures of supply and demand, do not of themselves supply the necessary degree of protection. Increasingly the supply side is coming to be or is held in the hands of a decreasing number of large concerns which are in the position to use economic power in a way that is not available to the thousands of individual economic consumers.
The new and complex technology going into consumer goods makes it increasingly difficult if not impossible for the consumer to make meaningful judgments as to their quality and safety. The same problem is created by much of modern packaging which, while attractive and colourful, provides a very limited amount of or no real information as to the contents of the package and its quantity. And even the information that is provided is often in a form that makes it impossible for the average person to make any meaningful comparison between the particular product and other products he may be interested in purchasing, unless he has a slide rule and an advanced degree in economics, biochemistry or dietetics.
If products may not be bought with safety it is obviously no answer to say to the consumer, "You do not have to buy this product next time." The damage is already done. In fact, the damage is done even where it is only a matter of the price of the particular product not being justified by the quality which the consumer finds when he opens the package. After all, the consumer's money is gone; and if it is a big ticket item, an expensive appliance, for example, it will be a long time before that consumer, who is stuck with something that does not measure up to the standards he was led to believe he could expect, will be able to go into the market again.
There have been continuing and growing complaints about rises in food costs, about misleading packaging, labelling and advertising, and about the difficulties consumers have in making judgments in a meaningful way when about to make purchases, as well as the organized consumer protests of the past several years. These show that our market economy, in spite of its obvious achievements in providing an amazing range of goods for a large number of people, does not of itself contain, adequate mechanisms to protect consumers from being misled or abused. This, of course, has been partially recognized over
October 20. 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs the years, as evidenced by the creation at federal and provincial levels of legislation such as the food and drug laws and the weights and measures laws which are designed to afford a degree of protection to the consumer. At the federal level, however, as has been pointed out, responsibility for implementing and administering this legislation has been scattered over a number of branches, over a number of different departments, all of which have other primary purposes and concerns. There are gaps which have not been covered by existing legislation. There has been no central co-ordination, no voice for the consumer interest at the policy-making level.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, will go a long way to meeting these requests. The bill creating the department of consumer affairs is one that has been requested by the Canadian Consumers Association for a number of years. The report of the joint committee of the house and Senate on consumer prices, a committee created by this government, strongly recommended the creation of such a department. Obviously there will be an important role for the new department of corporate and consumer affairs, not only to carry out more effectively existing programs of consumer protection but to add to them and expand them where necessary.
The federal government-and I should like to deal with a number of areas of activity which I hope might be undertaken by this new department-already sets standards for many products it buys. Many of these products are also offered by their manufacturers to the consumer market. Why cannot the federal government go on to expand its existing program of setting standards and set standards which would cover a wider range of goods? It could offer a mark which could be carried by goods meeting these standards. The government has gone part of the way in the area of marking agricultural products. Even there, consumer groups have pointed out the need for making these markings more immediately meaningful and significant to the consumer. Therefore I suggest that one program that might well be undertaken by this new department would be to expand the system of standards which already covers a wide range of products purchased by the federal government. In that way a marking could be made available to products meeting these standards offered to the consumer.
Surely, also, there is room for the strengthening of existing laws to ensure fair and informative labelling of goods to permit meaningful comparisons to be made. Sometimes

we hear arguments that abuses in labelling, packaging and advertising can be left to the self-regulation of the appropriate segment of industry, to the segment of the business community that is concerned. I think the available evidence proves that this is certainly not the answer.
Better business bureaux do good work but the great gap there, of course, is that they have no sanctions they can apply to those who they find have not met the minimum standards required. I have had people come to me and say "I went to the better business bureau and they wrote a letter to the firm; the firm did not reply or they gave an unsatisfactory answer and the better business bureau says that it is sorry but it cannot do any more."
This shows that in spite of many satisfactory adjustments bodies such as better business bureaux are able to obtain there are gaps which cannot be filled by such voluntary adjustment programs. Sometimes an industry group comes along and says, "We have set up an association; we have a code of conduct, and it is going to do the trick". Of course, the weakness of this argument is that a code of standards of this type has no effect on the firm that does not believe in it or that does not want to follow it. I think that reference has already been made to the code of standards set up by what I believe is called the Canadian Association of Manufacturers of Chemical Products. It is a very useful code, but it is one which would have no effect on those firms that do not choose to belong to the association or which choose to belong to it but say that they do not care to carry out this code in its entirety.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the minister of this new department, if it is approved by parliament as I hope it will be, could look into the creation of a body within his department to carry out a task somewhat similar to that carried out by the federal trade commission in the United States.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Our systems of enterprise and of industry are not so dissimilar that the type of complaints with which this body deals in the United States, complaints concerned with misleading advertising, misleading packaging and so forth, could not be found to exist here. So there is room at the federal level for action. I think there could be jurisdiction under the existing laws governing patents and trade marks. I suspect jurisdiction will be found also under the heading of the British North America Act covering trade and
October 20, 1967

commerce. Some students of the matter have said that this power could be used far more actively and creatively than it has been up til now. I hope the minister will take a look at these studies if he has not already done so, and that he will be influenced by their conclusions.
1 hope, also that the minister will take steps to make some of the facilities of the various government laboratories such as exist in the National Research Council available for the testing of consumer products. I understand it is very difficult for consumer groups in Canada to have tests carried out, such is the expense involved, and I maintain that if firms making industrial products can turn to the N.R.C. and ask for tests to be carried out in connection with the manufacture of their products, active consideration should be given to allowing laboratory facilities to be used for the testing of consumer products to provide better information for consumers.
Since we have jurisdiction over promissory notes and bills of exchange I think people are on the right track when they say the federal government should help eliminate the abuses which occur when finance companies, having taken assignment of promissory notes, hide behind the non-recourse provision in the Bills of Exchange Act and say to consumers whose goods have fallen short of reasonable standards-perhaps they have never even received the goods ordered- "We can do nothing for you; you have signed a document without recourse and that is all there is to it." Some nice legal points are involved in all this, but it is too much to expect the average citizen to be aware of all the implications of this type of purchase arrangement and I think there is room for corrective action to be taken under the leadership of the minister and his new department.
I hope, too, that the creation of this new department will mean the carrying on under federal jurisdiction of the progress reflected in the Bank Act where provision is now made for disclosure of the true interest rates on loans. At the present time this is limited to borrowing from banks under the Bank Act. There is room for amendment to the present Small Loans Act to make sure that people who borrow within the terms of that act are able to know the real cost of their borrowing. This is a subject on which the joint committee on the cost of living and consumer credit, again under the leadership of Senator Croll and the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) did a lot of
Corporate and Consumer Affairs constructive work, and it represents an important field of action for the new department.
I urge that the jurisdiction over combines will be actively used to ensure that the trend to bigness on the part of manufacturers and suppliers will in fact bring the benefits of mass production and mass distribution to consumers rather than become the basis of inordinate price increases.
There is certainly something to be said for educating the consumer, but there is obviously a role for regulation too, and this must be the justification for including in the responsibilities of the new department jurisdiction over certain federal responsibilities in the area of corporate affairs-bankruptcy, patents, trade marks and so on. The protection of consumer interests on the demand side requires regulatory activity on the supply side as well. I might add that this type of activity is also a protection for businessmen who want to provide quality goods at reasonable prices. Possibly the minister has seen a note in the recent edition of Consumer Reports suggesting that a sort of Gresham's law of the marketplace is in operation whereby the existence of a large number of people producing shoddy goods discourages more reputable businessmen from turning out goods of better quality at reasonable prices.
It seems to me that if the purpose of including these regulatory activities in the work of the department is to protect the consumer interest the name of the department should be reversed and it should be called the department of consumer and corporate affairs, not the department of corporate and consumer affairs. Even though certain business regulatory activities are provided for, my contention is that the basic purpose of the department is to protect the consumer interest, and I think this can be taken from the remarks of the minister himself. I note that as reported on page 3069 of Hansard for October 13, the hon. member said:
In order to represent the demand side of the marketplace and to give the consumer and investor a direct voice in governmental affairs, any department charged with that responsibility would have to have some authority over certain aspects of the supply side of the marketplace. Those aspects of the supply side of the marketplace are covered within the corporate affairs functions of this department.
I note also that as reported on page 3108 the minister said:
I hope that this department will be responsible to the consumer, will represent the consumer and will give the consumer a new voice at the ministerial level of the federal government.
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
If this is the intention of the minister and of the government I suggest to him and to the house that as soon as we reach the committee stage on this legislation the name of the proposed new department be amended so that it will clearly be demonstrated that the emphasis in this department is placed where it should be, that is, on caring for the interests of the consumer. I myself would be happy to move an appropriate amendment if this were acceptable. I strongly urge on the minister and the house acceptance of the idea of putting the word "consumer" first in the name of the department so as to demonstrate that this government is assuming its responsibility to exercise as completely as possible its jurisdiction in a meaningful way to protect an interest common to all Canadians-our interest as consumers.

That was a narrow squeak, Mr. Speaker; I have just finished writing a few notes in connection with this bill.
First, I should like to congratulate the hon. gentleman on his coming appointment to this most important ministry and wish him well in all he undertakes in the administration of this legislation when it becomes law. In that connection I may say I have been asked by some of the people who knew him when he was a young man to extend their best wishes as well.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
This and previous debates within the last two weeks have indicated that similar problems come repeatedly before the house. This is an indication that history repeats itself. I am rather fond of history. I suppose that is why on occasion I am called a bit of an old Victorian, but I do not mind that.
It is interesting to note that on April 16, 1935, the house discussed the first federal housing policy. We have heard about housing policy in recent days. On April 12, 1935, the house discussed the radio broadcasting bill. We have a bill dealing with that subject before the house at the present time. On April 9, 1935, the house amended the Post Office Act, and in the near future we expect another bill to amend that act. On April 12, 1935, the house discussed the price spreads commission report. I well remember reading that report when it was issued. I well remember the interest created throughout the country as a result of the hearings that the commission held.

speechtext: Does the hon. member know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was the secretary of that commission?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext: I had forgotten, but now I remember he was. I also well remember that that commission was established as a result of the activity of Hon. H. H. Stevens, a Conservative member of parliament, who was concerned about the depressed economic condition of the country at the time. We must give him credit. He was the first one to campaign in an election to form a new party, the Reconstruction party. He was elected in Kootenay East and his election slogan was, "Protect the Consumers' Interests." He spoke on that subject in the house, as did other hon. members on both sides of the house. The issue was boiling at that time. It was of great interest to the Canadian people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext: Conservatives are always interested in the well being of the consumers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
I would naturally suppose so. However, owing to improved economic conditions and to the second world war, interest in that issue died. Now we are faced with a similar round of circumstances, with a rising cost of living over the last few years which has again brought the matter to the attention of the house. A committee of the house has given considerable thought to the question and has heard witnesses from consumers' associations and other groups. I only mention these things to indicate that there seems to be a continuing cycle in parliamentary affairs as a result of which problems return to us over a period of years.
I listened with interest to the minister's speech and to the speeches made by members of this group. There is no necessity for me to repeat the criticisms that have already been stated with respect to the terms of the legislation. They were expressed forcefully and I am sure made an impact on the minister's mind. I also listened with interest to what I thought was a most constructive speech by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), dealing with the difficulties surrounding this type of legislation. Further, I listened to the interesting speech made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson). I thought he made an excellent speech and made some constructive suggestions with respect to the administration of the legislation.
In my opinion this bill does focus attention on a problem which is Canada-wide. The hon. member for Newfoundland mentioned that people in Newfoundland suffer more
October 20, 1967

from increases in the cost of living than we do in British Columbia, but the problem is country-wide and affects consumers in general.
I doubt that this legislation can be administered satisfactorily or will prove of great value unless the government is able to get the co-operation of the provincial governments in administering it. This point was mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River and other hon. members. I think that is essential. In the first instance there must be co-operation with respect to research, the providing of information and so on. It is also essential to have co-operation with consumer and other groups. The government must get the co-operation of larger groups in our society that are directly affected by increases in the cost of living. These would include consumer groups, women's organizations, trade unions, chambers of commerce and all other agencies that can be persuaded to co-operate with the federal government in giving effect to the legislation.
I trust the minister will accept the advice of hon. members who have suggested that information be given to the public on prices prevailing throughout the country, and that he will have courage enough to mention the names of firms that violate the spirit and intent of the legislation. In that respect I refer to brand names and company names. It is essential to focus attention on the culprit, no matter how important he happens to be in Canadian society. There is nothing as effective as drawing attention to the person who is causing problems for the people and the government.
I was most interested in references that were made to the need for an educational program. There again we must get the cooperation of all interested groups. The public has got to be educated with respect to buying food which is of value because of its nutritional content. The public must also be educated on sound purchasing habits. There is a lot that can be done in that respect. We live in a very wasteful society. We see this every day, and I think something can be done by the federal government, provincial governments and other agencies to help establish sounder habits in that respect.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned baking one's own bread. This is something very dear to my heart. I realize that a great number of women are working today and do not have the opportunity to bake

Corporate and Consumer Affairs their own bread, but from practical experience I know they can do it. My wife bakes her own bread even here in Ottawa with only two of us to eat it. We have kept track of the cost of homemade bread and I can tell you the cost is about half that of baker's bread.
I think the minister would be well advised to get in touch even with people on welfare who are going to shops and buying expensive baker's bread in order to see to it that they are given information on how to bake their own bread.
