speechtext:
I think the department
should arrange for competent officials to give talks to women's institutes, consumer groups, farm organizations, chambers of commerce, in fact to any groups willing to listen to government policy and learn what it hopes to achieve. In this way such groups will participate in the work. This is a suggestion which I have made with reference to other legislation. I forget for the moment which legislation it was, but at any rate the department concerned followed the advice and it was surprising the co-operation it got from various organizations once they had an opportunity to listen to the government's policy.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We must remember that this is a large country. Many of our towns and smaller communities have a feeling of being a long way from the centre of government. I think it would be a good thing if they were given the feeling that they are involved in the administration of legislation. This could be accomplished at least in part by their being informed through the lectures which I suggest and in other ways.
I believe it is very necessary for the minister to co-operate with the press. I doubt that it is necessary for me to advise him in this regard because he is an intelligent young man. I must say that I have heard several references to a certain image being created. I do not agree with that. I loathe the word "image" because it is a product of Madison avenue attempts to deceive people for the
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs purpose of selling goods, services or personalities. I am sure the minister is above that. I suggest that there should be every co-operation with the press here in this house and throughout the country, as well as with the farm union periodicals. I think this idea must be sold to them. If they are genuine in their expressed concern about the cost of living and its impact on the Canadian people generally, they should be only too willing to cooperate and place the research they have done on this matter in the hands of the federal and other governments which require it.
As I said before, there is a great deal to be done in connection with research as a result of co-operation between all governments and agencies which can do effective work in this direction. As a result such research will provide a basis for information which may be given to the Canadian people.
Before I take my seat I should like to deal broadly with clause 5 which reads as follows:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister extend to and include all matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, not by law assigned to any other department, branch or agency of the government of Canada...
Those are pretty wide terms of reference. Then it goes on to say that this provision relates to certain matters. The first is consumer affairs, which I have been discussing for a few minutes. The next is corporations and corporate securities. I think other members who have spoken have given us the benefit of their knowledge and opinions on that question.
Then there is reference to combines, mergers, monopolies and restraint of trade. There is a general feeling abroad that the combines investigation branch, giving it all credit for the work it has done in the past, has not been as effective as it should be in prohibiting combines and mergers throughout this country. I am sure the minister will explore all avenues by which the administration of this legislation may be improved.
The next is bankruptcy and involvency. I have had a little experience in respect of bankruptcies. I have been a trustee in bankruptcy and that sort of thing. On one occasion when I was an inspector I refused to sign the report which was being made to the superintendent of bankruptcy by the trustee in question because I said it was not true. Nothing was done about this. It was sent to Ottawa and that was the last I heard about it. For some unknown reason and because of my stubbornness in refusing to sign the

report, apparently it was decided that it would be accepted without my signature. This was done.
There is need for a different state of affairs in respect of the administration of bankruptcies at this time. This is a problem which is more widespread than would appear on the surface. Justice must be done with regard to all parties who are concerned. I trust the minister will tighten up the administration of bankruptcies after this legislation is adopted.
Then we come to patents, copyrights and trade marks. I have had experience in this regard, but I have no criticism to make of the branch of the minister's new department which will be responsible for this aspect because I have found that generally these matters have been handled well and if they were in confidence and so on they were treated in that way.
I believe that the matters which have been stressed are ones in respect of which something must be done to protect the consumers of this country and to strengthen the Bankruptcy Act so that it will be administered fairly in respect of all persons concerned with any bankruptcy. I do not intend to say much more at this time because as I said before I do not believe in repeating unnecessarily what has already been said. In conclusion may I say that I for one will be looking forward with the hope, as will other Canadians, that the minister will be able to make this department really effective, because attention is focused on this department, on this legislation and on its administration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length because I know this very important bill has been discussed objectively and constantly since Tuesday. I know also that hon. members who have spoken and who have taken a keen interest in this debate so far would like, if possible, to wind up the debate today so that the minister will have an opportunity to express his opinions and obtain second reading before the normal closing time.
I am particularly pleased at this time to have an opportunity to participate in the debate because of the fact that the minister and I both come from the island of Montreal. We were elected to the House of Commons in the same general election of 1962. We shared the same office and, indeed, since there was only one telephone for two members in those days we shared the same telephone during
October 20, 1967

the short period of time when we sat on the opposition side between 1962 and 1963.
I think the minister will prove to be extremely capable in the administration of his department. Although we sometimes forget this fact he has been a member of the House of Commons now for five years. During that time he has shown considerable interest in the policies and affairs of the nation. He has also built up a reputation, which is fully deserved, as a very objective and progressive member of the government. I am sure it is the feeling of every person in this house that he will do justice to this very important department.
There has been some criticism to the effect that in many ways this bill does not go far enough. One must take into consideration, however, the rather peculiar make-up of this country and the obvious necessity for the government to respect our constitution. This is a point which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) emphasized so eloquently earlier today. Many of the problems with which we are confronted in 1967 and which tend to create a feeling of disunity and resentment in this country have arisen from the fact that too often in the past we have been prone to disregard the spirit and intent of the constitution as it was envisaged 100 years ago.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
So, Mr. Speaker, the effectiveness of this department in many areas will depend on the persuasive talents of the minister and the team of experts he is rapidly attracting to this new and all-important department. I presume and hope that the future of this nation will depend more and more on a greater degree of co-operation among all three levels of government. I believe this will all come about because the public is becoming more aware of the problems which tend to create disunity. They are growing impatient with politicians at different levels who attempt to hide behind the constitution. I suspect that the people of Canada very properly anticipate and expect more co-operation and joint action, particularly in respect of the affairs of the consumers and those things important to the man on the street, than has been the custom in the past.
Rather than being pessimistic about the fact that in some ways this bill depends on more co-operation between federal and provincial authorities, I am optimistic because I think this is the spirit that will prevail in Canada in the future. It is my belief that the
Corporate and Consumer Affairs federal government will respect the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and that this will become a country in which provincial governments in turn will realize the necessity for closer co-operation and greater communication with the government here in Ottawa.
I followed with a great degree of interest, as I am sure most members did, the events leading up to the establishment of this department. I read with great interest and concern the proceedings of the joint committee of the house and the Senate on consumer affairs. The many facts brought out by that particular committee were very revealing. They indicated the need to make practices more uniform, less confusing and less deceptive. It will be the role and the responsibility of the minister to rectify these obvious misrepresentations which do occur from time to time in what has been commonly called the marketplace.
I am not in accord with those people who have expressed the opinion here, outside the house and before the committee, that advertising is bad, that it adds to the cost of production and that if we could eliminate or limit advertising we would automatically reduce the price of the commodity. Nothing is further from the truth. Advertising in general has played a very important role in the development of the economy of the North American continent. It is in fact one of the fundamental and basic differences between our economy and that prevalent behind the iron curtain, where advertising until very recently was practically non-existent. It is significant as we travel around the world to see other countries adopting the marketing practices which are prevalent in the United States, and indeed in Canada. They are being adopted because they are logical.
We are all nostalgic about the old fashioned marketplaces, but the majority of housewives prefer to buy their produce today from the supermarkets rather than from outlets such as are still prevalent in many parts of Europe, where they count out so many heads of corn, and measure and weigh everything to be placed in a paper bag for the customer. That was the situation when I was young-and I am not that old.
Let me point out to the minister that I hope during his remarks he will assure the house and the public that he is interested in the advertising world, that he will not limit advertising on the pretense of preventing fraud or deceptive advertising. I hope he will
October 20, 196?

Corporate and Consumer Affairs assure us that he has no intention of limiting or interfering with private enterprise by suggesting that a part of their advertising budget over and above a certain ceiling be allocated to cost reductions.
In this regard I have in mind the drug industry. The Hall commission report suggested that drug advertising should be limited. This is the type of restriction intended to lower the cost of drugs, but I suggest it would be a flagrant interference in what to this date has been private enterprise. Even the arch-enemies of the drug industry from the United States who appeared before the committee made the point that there would certainly be little or no purpose in curtailing advertising.
When referring to volume advertising, the money spent cannot be associated only with the advertising field. Many loose statements have been made about advertising and the need to curtail, restrict or interfere with it. One has only to consider the cost of the daily newspaper to realize the very valuable role that advertising plays in our everyday life. We are all aware of the fact that we could not buy a newspaper for seven cents, 10 cents or even 15 cents were it not for the revenue from advertising. Our radio and television stations could not operate efficiently or economically without the support of advertising. Again I am not referring to distasteful or fraudulent advertising. I am emphasizing that advertising has played an important role in the development of our economy. This is one of the main differences between the economy of this country and countries such as Poland and Russia.
In this respect it is interesting to note the news from Poland, Russia and other iron curtain countries which indicates that they are going to do things in a different way in the marketing world. They intend to pattern their methods after those prevalent in this part of the world. I suggest to the minister that he resist any effort on the part of his advisors, if indeed there are any such efforts being made, to adopt any restrictive action in respect of advertising. He should not adopt any restrictive measures in this regard, other than those of laying down rules and regulations governing what constitutes honest as opposed to dishonest advertising.
I should like to have said more about other things in relation to this subject, but I realize it is now four o'clock and that one of the more active members of the consumers committee wants to make a few remarks. I also realize that the minister would like to


conclude the debate. Therefore, I will stress one point rather than the three or four I had in mind.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am very pleased to note that clause 5 of the bill, which refers to other duties of the minister, does not cover such typical things as the price of cornflakes, whether the boxes should be red, blue or green, oblong or square. The minister has retained, as he should, some other very important responsibilities. I am referring, for instance, to patents, copyrights and trade marks. I am very much aware of these because, along with other hon. members, I attended close to 100 meetings of the special committee on food and drugs and we all realize that there is no cut and dried solution in this very complicated field. But I would remind the minister that out of the Harley committee report came, not one or two, but 21 or 22 or more recommendations. I am not sure of precisely how many there were because I have not looked at them for several months.
One of the problems of the government, which is perhaps at times an indication of a lack of communication between different ministers, is that to implement all the recommendations of the Harley committee report which, if they were all introduced, would achieve the desired effect of lowering the cost of drugs, would require the efforts not only of the present minister whose department we are discussing but also legislation by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and perhaps the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). In all fairness to the pres-sent minister I think that before making important changes, for instance in the field of patents, copyrights and trade marks, he should discuss them with the other ministers involved, because he may find these desirable changes are not practicable and cannot be effective unless another minister brings forward necessary legislation.
In that same report it was proposed that the recommendations of the Hilliard report be implemented and that before the minister decides to adopt certain recommendations of the Harley committee to alter the Patent Act, the Copyright Act or the Trade Marks Act he should make certain that the food and drug directorate is enlarged and given the proper funds to ensure that the drugs flowing into this country as a result of these changes are subjected to the most rigid scrutiny. I am not
October 20, 1967

a medical man but I read the report, I attended the meetings and I understood the implications of the Hilliard report. The Hilliard report simply states that the methods of inspection in Canada today are not stringent enough and that they should be more sophisticated.
I may remind members of the house that this committee was set up as a result of a request made in the house by Dr. Jones, a former member. I should say, in all fairness to the minister, that if he were to introduce changes in the Patent Act without previously ascertaining that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will implement the Hilliard report and that the same minister will broaden the food and drug directorate so as to provide an assurance to the Canadian public that the imports coming into the country as a result of these changes are subjected to the most rigid tests in order to avoid another thalidomide tragedy or something of this nature, he would be doing a disservice to the Canadian public. The point I am trying to make is that as a member of the Harley committee and as one who endorsed its recommendations I am convinced that changes to the Patent Act will entail provisions which would give greater importance to the safety of drugs than to their cost.
I think the minister understands my message and agrees with me that the cost of drugs must and can be reduced by proper legislation but it cannot be reduced by piecemeal legislation. So there should be a concentrated effort on the part of all the ministers involved to implement the recommendations of the Harley report almost simultaneously, otherwise we would be unfair to the minister of this all-important new department.
I might say, as a personal friend of the minister, as one who was elected in the island of Montreal at the same time as he was and as one who shared the same office during the short time we were in opposition, that I wish him well. I know he will make a success of this department and I suggest to those people who feel this bill does not go far enough that we must not underestimate the minister's well known persuasive ability to acquire or achieve the right degree of co-operation from the provincial and civic authorities

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to go over a great deal of the ground that has been traversed these last few days, but I do not want to see second reading given to this bill without making a few comments in summary, because in my view the matter
Corporate and Consumer Affairs dealt with in the consumer part of the bill is one of the most important to come before parliament this fall. I consider it, along with housing, as being of first urgency in the minds of the people across the country. I want to make certain points crystal clear because now that we are committed to this legislation there is no particular point in trying to do other than to see what it will do and where it falls short.
I should like to point out the genesis of this legislation. A year ago women from all across Canada, buyers and shoppers for their families, found that the cost of living had risen out of all proportion. They came in large numbers from all across Canada to picket and boycott the supermarkets of this country. They made their voices well heard and their influence well felt on parliament hill. It was because of them and nothing else that the committee which was set up to study consumer credit was instructed to study the cost of living, which it did with particular reference to food and to a lesser extent to housing. I want to emphasize that this legislation was brought down first and foremost because of the rising cost of living.
The committee found there were two problems of great urgency to the customers of this country. One was the problem of consumer standards. The other was a problem of infinitely greater concern and urgency, namely the problem of the rising prices. When we were first given a chance to look at this bill most of us had the feeling that it empowered the new department to do something about consumer standards. However, on looking at it more closely we see that it is vague in its terms although it allows the minister to deal with standards, and such things as deceptive packaging, labelling and deceptive advertising. I do not want to belittle this aspect of the bill. I think it is important to all consumers across Canada that there be legislation dealing with deception and false advertising.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Having said that I should now like to point out that this legislation attempts to do little or nothing at all to deal with the really urgent problem facing the consumers of this country, namely the rising cost of living. This bill is particularly empty in that regard. Unfortunately, I was not able to listen to the minister's speech at the second reading stage of the bill. However, I read it quite carefully hoping to find that he would put some teeth into that part of the legislation which should be dealing with prices. I hoped he would be able to read something into the legislation
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs having to do with prices and the cost of living. Unfortunately, I consider the minister's speech was a little like the deceptive packaging and labelling about which we have heard. I thought his speech cast a veil of uncertainty and confusion around the legislation instead of helping to clarify it.
I do not believe the minister made any case that he intends to do anything about the cost of living, other than the slight savings that might accrue to the consumer as a result of improved packaging and labelling. Those things, Mr. Speaker, the deceptive packaging and labelling, are less than one tenth of the iceberg that shows above the water. The danger to navigation lies in that part of the iceberg below the waterline, that part which cannot be seen, and I would compare it to the cost of living. I am afraid that when we have eliminated the glossy packaging of the minister's speech we are left with the conclusion that we will have empty hands, in so far as our fight against the cost of living is concerned.
I am afraid that the picture the one hon. member drew this morning of a very gallant Mr. Turner accompanying the housewife through the supermarket with her shopping buggy, protecting her from the cost of living as they went along from shelf to shelf, will not remain long with Mrs. Consumer across the country. I think that after all the foufa-raw of the debate, it will be seen that the minister has taken refuge, as the ministers of other departments have before him, behind the constitutional difficulty of doing this job of coming to grips with the cost of living.
We are not denying for a moment that this is exceedingly difficult. It is a piece of pioneering. Never before in peacetime have we had to come to grips with the problems of the cost of living and prices, in the way we have to do now. In his speech the other day the minister indicated that I seemed to be looking upon the new department as a reincarnation of the wartime prices control board. I am not looking upon it as that at all. I am under no illusion that the new department pretends to be a reincarnation of the wartime prices control board, nor at this stage do I want it to be such. I do want to reprimand the minister, and I say this more in sorrow than in anger, because he has said very clearly he does not intend to cope with these difficulties.
It is the minister's unwillingness, his folding up in front of the difficulties, constitutional and otherwise, which I feel is regrettable.

We know the constitutional difficulties are great. Pioneering has to be done. We know also that in every province from Newfoundland to British Columbia there are thousands upon thousands of families on low incomes, families with a large number of children, people who are on welfare, old age pensioners, people who are incapacitated, and so on, who are groaning under the burden of the rising cost of living. This morning one of the members from Newfoundland referred to the difficulties in that province. I want to say, as I said at the resolution stage, that if the minister would take his courage in both hands and go to these provinces, they could devise machinery at the federal and provincial levels, whether it be concurrent legislation or some other type of machinery, with which to deal with the rising cost of living. We would get some stability for the consumer. I do not believe there would be a provincial government that would dare say no to such a suggestion.
Everyone says that this minister is young, vigorous and energetic. Heaven knows he has that appearance, and I hope it is not just an appearance. I hope he will use these qualities of youth and energy in order to do the pioneering job that needs to be done. I say to the minister that in all the important fields today what we need is not a federal government quarrelling with provincial governments, like dogs daring each other to step into the other's territory. This attitude has been tried and has been found wanting today. What we need is a partnership between the federal government and the provinces in order to find ways and means of dealing with an urgent problem. Housing and the cost of living are two of the most urgent problems. I should like the minister to try to find a workable solution with the provinces. He could go to them one by one or take them on all at once if he felt capable of doing so. He may find one that would be receptive. Ontario might be a good place to start because that province proved amenable to working with the federal government in connection with housing. I do not see why they would not do so in this case. Recently the Ontario government has had a reminder that if they do not, somebody else will, and in the not too distant future. I believe ways and means could be worked out for controlling this cost of living.
I knew the minister had been reading Mr. Galbraith's book the minute he spoke about the split level facet of our economy. I knew that although he used his own language to
October 20, 1967	COMMONS
describe the economy. I hope he will not disappoint me by saying he has not read the book. The minister knows quite well that all corporations in this country are not subject to the free play of the market. He knows the giant corporations which dominate every major field of Canadian industry are able to plan right down to the last detail. They are, to a very great extent, independent of market influence. He knows that they can plan their budget, they can plan their returns, and he knows that advertising cannot be dealt with separately because advertising is an integral part of their existence. He knows all these things.
But I should like to suggest to the minister there is something he does not know. Mrs. Consumer, from one coast to the other, wants to be able to plan her budget, too. The consumers of this country have been unable to plan their budgets because they have been subjected to uncontrolled advertising which has pulled their budget entirely out of control. As a result of these different merchandising interests jockeying for a larger share of the housewife's dollar, her budget has gotten completely out of balance.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
She finds she is no longer able to purchase those items which are essential to a decent standard of living in this country. What is required is to get some kind of price stability for the consumers of this country. We need this type of planning in the homes of this country. The people of this country are looking to this government for the opportunity to make a balanced, planned budget for their families, just as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is expected to do for the nation as a whole. I very much wish that the minister would attempt to do this.
We will, of course, Mr. Speaker, have to support this legislation because it does take care of the standards problem, at least in a measure. But we are going to support it very reluctantly and half-heartedly because of what the legislation does not do. During the committee stage we will try to improve it if we can. On the other hand, we feel there are many problems in connection with the cost of living that are not even touched by this legislation.
If the minister cannot do any better than what is envisaged in this legislation, then I do not think it will be very long before the consumers of this country once again start to boycott supermarkets and other merchants. This they will have to do. Consumers have
DEBATES	3345
Corporate and Consumer Affairs been asking me all along the line what this new legislation is going to do to reduce the cost of living.
One good aspect about this legislation, to which I would like to refer, is the intention of the minister to provide consumer information. I hope that this will not be given in stodgy, unimaginative leaflet form in this day and age, when radio and television are the media for contacting people. I should like to see the minister use our information facilities to the full.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if he really wants to become known and to make his mark in Canada among people who have never cared very much for politics-and I refer to the women of this country-then this is one way he can do so. The reason that women in this country have never cared very much for politics is not difficult to see. They have been burdened of course with the greater share of caring for children in the home. But even at that, Mr. Speaker, if women wanted to be interested in politics this double burden would not stop them. The reason the women of this country have not been interested in politics is that they have failed to see the connection between politics and family concerns, such as the welfare of their husbands, their children and their homes.
I suggest to the minister, at risk of telling him how to prolong the life of this government, that if he wants to make a name for himself and to help his own followers in the government nothing he may say would be half as important as to up and grapple with this problem of the cost of living in general, and of prices in particular. Let him enter this den of lions, the provinces, if I may call them that, and approach them as though they are not going to bite. And perhaps they will not, Mr. Speaker, because they are under the gun, too.
If the minister would do this and amend the legislation accordingly, and if he were willing to listen to some amendments which will be moved from the floor, then I believe he will have left an enduring mark not only upon the political scene of the country but, what is far more important, in the hearts of the people of the country who so very desperately need protection at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the debate during the last two or three
3346	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs days and noted the path which it has taken. I want to thank members of the house for their active participation in the discussion of this bill, and to thank particularly those members of the house who wanted to speak this afternoon but who agreed to defer their remarks until clause 2, which we will reach on the committee stage. I appreciate this very much. I think it has been a good debate, if not wholly constructive in every element. I should like to deal with two or three of the issues which have been raised, if I might, before I reply in general terms to some of the questions and objections that were raised during the course of our discussions.
First, Mr. Speaker, let me say to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that I was particularly interested in the position taken by the Conservative party. I felt that they were developing a new style of activity in this house, one which I would call a flip-flop, acrobatic style of politics. I mean by that that they are a party that have changed their course in midstream.
I recall having sat through the resolution stage last Friday and listened to the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). The chief opposition party at that time was taking the view that a department of consumer affairs was not necessary at all. I have only to refer to the words of the hon. member for Yukon, reported at page 3073 of Hansard:
In essence we on this side of the house believe that the government is not following a prudent course in setting up a new department to deal with the growing and vexing problem of consumer affairs in this country.
The hon. member for Peace River used words to similar effect, to be found at page 3086.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we find during the course of this debate, and in particular in the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon who opened on behalf of the official opposition, that he has disagreed with himself and has now become awfully concerned that the legislation setting up this department has not gone far enough.
This leads me to the question, why the change of heart? I have been pondering that question and wondering whether it was the discovery of the Gallup poll published earlier in the week, which in effect indicated that control of profits, prices and the cost of living had in the minds of the Canadian people become of primary concern to consumers. All I want to say in this regard is: What a difference three days make. At the resolution

DEBATES	October 20, 1967
stage there was severe doubt about the necessity for a department at all. Then on second reading stage there is the feeling that the department as constituted does not go far enough: No consistency, no coherence.

speechtext:
I think that the government was persuaded as to the importance of this particular problem in that it introduced this legislation, and I think the legislation will speak for itself.
I also listened with great interest to the very reasoned speech today of the hon. member for Peace River. His argument was that in order to accomplish what in his view the bill attempts to accomplish-I trust I am stating his argument fairly-a bill was not necessary at all. To his mind everything could have been accomplished in a reorganization bill; that the only purpose of a bill was to give the department a new name. I think in essence that was his argument.
In the view of the government this bill establishes in clear and definable terms the presence of the federal government in the consumer field.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order, because when the minister finishes at five o'clock I will not be able to speak again. I did say that was the case if it was intended to take only the narrow, more restricted position with regard to the government's intentions. On the other hand, I went on to say that if there was a real intention on the part of the government to try to come to grips with the wider problem of price control, I suggested certain measures by which the government could achieve this intention.

speechtext:
I will of course accept that explanation, Mr. Speaker; none the less the argument is on the record and I feel I should answer it.
The purpose of this bill is to establish in clear and definable terms the presence of the federal government and of this department in the consumer field. The bill establishes authority to co-ordinate and to represent the consumer interest. I think that the people of Canada have a right to know what are the purposes of the department and the methods that are being used to achieve those purposes. It is because of this that we have
October 20, 1967	COMMONS
attempted to define quite clearly in clause 6 of the legislation just what this scope will be within the complex of the federal government.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Let me say to the hon. member for Peace River, who like myself is a lawyer, that this legislation is not merely a legal document but a statement of government intention. As the ordinary citizen in this country is apprised of that intention through the communications media he will know what the government is intending to do. I feel that in his argument the hon. member took a narrow and juridical approach. In the amendment to the transportation bill especially, in section 2, the government set out the national transportation policy of Canada so that the people of this country would know how the government felt about that national policy. Also, in the broadcasting bill there is a declaratory section which sets out national broadcasting policy. Section 6 of the bill sets out, in clear language, the government's intentions with respect to this department. Government is not only the art of doing things; it is also the art of accepting responsibility for doing them. This bill pinpoints that responsibility in a new focal point for the consumer.
I wish to deal briefly with the arguments of the New Democratic party. Basically, their argument is that this bill is window dressing, that this bill has no teeth. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said that I betrayed a nineteenth century philosophy in my concept of the marketplace, though he admitted that I had read Galbraith. He took an isolated remark from a speech that lasted one and a half hours.
My answer is that it is true, this bill does not set out the entire program for consumer affairs, as contemplated by the government. This bill is enabling legislation setting up a new department, having authority to co-ordinate existing activities; it is to promote the consumer interest and to initiate new measures. In my opening speech I described some possible measures to which parliament will be asked to assent to. I expect to be back in the house before too long with new legislation.
Answering the N.D.P., I believe that this department is a great step forward. I believe that the co-ordination of the consumer's interest will be more effective than it has been up to now. It has not been too effective because that co-ordination has been lacking. Existing consumer legislation is considerable in scope,

Corporate and Consumer Affairs and it will become more effective when certain new programs are introduced-programs such as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and others on her side of the house.

speechtext: What about prices?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall come to prices. As I said, and I direct my remarks to members of the New Democratic party particularly, already on the statute books there is a considerable quantity of legislation affecting consumers. All this legislation is less effective than it might be because of a lack of coordination. To bring about this co-ordination is part of the federal program with respect to consumer affairs. Here I am talking about section 306 of the Criminal Code and about section 33C of the Combines Investigation Act. These relate to misleading advertising, and so on. I also refer to the amendments to the Corporations Act. We shall be moving into the federal security field, for the protection of investors. We shall be making efforts to coordinate and consolidate legislation on consumer credit. Here I must also mention the food and drugs regulations that are already on the books, the weights and measures legislation that is already administered by the standards branch; the laws affecting the description of misleading or deceptive qualities, which are administered at the moment by the Departments of Agriculture and Fisheries; and, under the Combines Investigation Act, monopolies, mergers, restraint of trade, price fixing and retail inspection services will all be included. All this legislation will be coordinated; the welfare of the consumer will be paramount under new legislation.
This is not an omnibus bill; this is not a bill which contains the entire consumer program of the government. This is a bill that allows the department to co-ordinate the enforcement of all existing legislation.
I recognize, as I said in my opening speech, that intervention in the marketplace will be necessary. I think that I understand the nature of the large corporation and its dominant position in the marketplace. Historically, the legal corporation was given certain privileges under our statutes and common law. The concept of "limited liability" was an important economic innovation which galvanized fresh captial to take risks and embark on bold business adventures. The corporate veil became real in law and in fact. The inner workings of the corporation were hidden from public scrutiny and a wall of protection was built around the promoters and the
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs managers of our corporations. But the nature of the corporation has changed. There is now a separation between ownership and control, shareholders becoming more diverse. I believe the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) recited that fact. I believe it is clear that the average shareholder in Canada holds shares in any company for less than six months.
The average shareholder becomes a shareholder in transit; the real people over whom supervision is required are not the traditional owners of a corporation but those who manage it and control it, those whom Anthony Sampson referred as the paraproprietors.
The dramatic separation of control from ownership has changed the ground rules. We must adjust our vocabulary to the new circumstances. We must now pierce the corporate curtain and look behind it. The investing public must be properly formed and management made subject to reasonable guide lines. This department will intervene against the overwhelming market power of the corporation; it will penetrate the corporate veil. I wish to say that the department will pursue these aims with vigour.
I know that hon. members have read the recent report of the Director of Investigation and Research of the Combines branch. I admit that current legislation is somewhat inadequate. It is being reviewed by the Economic Council of Canada.
I wish to see jurisdiction extended into the service industries I wish to see a test made of the trade and commerce clause of the bill, so that we could use a civil solution as well as criminal remedies and not be restricted to the severe burden of truth enforced on us by the criminal law.
The merger sections are inadequate, as are those dealing with restrictive trade, and so on. As I said, the department does intend to enter the market with respect to fraud, deception, safety, conflict of interest situations, whether those might be between auditors, lawyers, trustees or others, and we shall act with respect to disclosure, insider trading, and so on.
The final argument, aside from the general one to do with costs of living, was the one raised by the New Democratic party about the prices review board. We were accused of drafting legislation that had no teeth; I deny that. I say to the leader of the N.D.P. that the prices review board would have no teeth in it. He as much as admitted this. He admitted that prices would be reviewed by the board,


but that the board would have no power to enforce its decisions. Its authority would be limited under federal jurisdiction, and he knew that. That is why he suggested, as a second step, concurrent provincial legislation.
I say to him that here we see a suggestion without teeth; here is a suggestion that is cumbersome. I wonder whether the hon. member has contemplated reviewing costs as well as wages; I wonder whether he has checked his idea with the labour movement? I believe that his proposal would, from the beginning, lack constitutional jurisdiction to back it.
I should like to deal with the cost of living and the role of the new department. Specifically I wish to deal with the question of prices which was of much concern not only to the opposition but to members on the government side also. I do not think there is anyone here who, knowing that others suffer under the burden of the increasing cost of living, is unaware of the extent of that burden. In this regard I think I speak for everyone in this house. Everyone in this house is concerned with rising prices and I suggest that it is irresponsible for the opposition to suggest that our attention is not seriously focussed on the problem.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Let me remind the house of some important facts which so far have been ignored by the opposition in its discussion of prices. Price movement is due to complex factors, many of which are beyond the control of the federal government. Some of them are beyond the control of the Canadian people generally. For example, international economic developments make a significant impact on prices; they are of severe consequence to us when one quarter of every dollar we earn is dependent on foreign trade. Spending both in the private sector and by provincial and municipal governments has also contributed to the very severe demand curve. We are also caught in a dilemma shared by every western government: full employment naturally means an upward pressure on prices and costs. We in this government have embarked on a policy of full employment, and this involves, as a corollary, risk to the stability of the cost of living. To quote from the third report of the economic council:
The most pervasive and recurrent goal conflict of modern industrial economies has proven to be that between full employment and reasonable stability of prices.
To meet these problems the government has used a careful orchestration of fiscal and
October 20. 1967

monetary policy. We have also attacked one of the basic causes of inflation, limited productivity, since increased productivity is the major means of escaping from rising prices.
Let me describe more fully the role of the new department. First of all, as I have said before in this house, the basic responsibility for any direct control of prices resides constitutionally with the provinces. This is not an escape valve; it happens to be a constitutional fact. This does not mean-and if I have given hon. members a wrong impression I will try to correct it, now-that the new department will not have a role. Hon. members know very well that in this department we are not responsible for the major instruments of fiscal policy which influence the general level of prices. However, as I made clear in my presentation, it is our intention to use the instruments we have wherever those instruments can be applied.
What are they? They include the use of the Combines Investigation Act and government machinery as a means of ensuring competition and fair trade. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) would read The Industrial State by John Galbraith more closely he would realize that Galbraith recognizes that the market relationship is still an important factor and that competition can be preserved or restored, through effective action against monopoly, to guard against excessive and artificial prices which exploit the consumer.
And where that exists, and where there are companies in a dominant position in any particular industry, and where that dominant position reaches a point at which prices may be influenced by one side of the market alone, or where a company may by its very size and dominance influence not only the price but the base of demand, and when that dominant position is reinforced by advertising so as to bring about almost a monopoly position, we shall be interested, we shall investigate, we shall act.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said that as far as he was concerned the existence of monopolies was a major cause of the rise in prices. I would be very glad to receive evidence of this from the hon. member; I am sure he would not say such a thing unless he did have evidence. I can tell him we would be glad to investigate any case of collusion or monopoly to which he can point specifically. If no evidence is available, I hope he will not accuse me of restricting the imaginative quality of his speech by drawing attention to a few facts. I am making no
Corporate and Consumer Affairs defence of the retail trade, but as a matter of fact, during the past five years-and I am quoting now from a report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which appeared in the Globe and Mail of October 19-the profit margin of the retail trade has fallen from 1.3 per cent to .8 per cent.
The facts seem to demonstrate against the hon. member's argument. However, as I say, if he has the evidence, let him present it to us or to the Director of Investigation and Research, and we shall look into it. I would point out, also, that we are strengthening the enforcement of anti-combines legislation, we are asking for bigger fines and we have asked the economic council to advise us on the modernization of the Combines Investigation Act so that it can be made even more effective.
In the second place, a primary reason in favour of the creation of a new department was the need to create a central body to examine and analyse selected areas of federal activities which can influence prices, and to take remedial action. There must be a ministry responsible for this function and it will be our purpose to seek out ways and means, other than those in the fiscal and monetary realm, by which the federal government can assist in the maintenance of price stability and in the reduction of prices. Our proposed legislation on drugs is an example of the way in which we can modify laws in order to help bring about lower prices. The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) asked about our intention with respect to drugs. All I can say is that we shall shortly introduce a bill to amend the legislation governing patents and trademarks.
The new department will also undertake investigation and research designed to produce information which will assist consumers to avoid excessive prices and to get the best value for their money. This is all the more necessary in the face of the confusion caused by the variety and complexity of consumer goods now being offered. Should it be felt that any particular study is required the government can of course, make use of its power under the Inquiries Act to get to the root of the problem.
For example, my department is already examining a problem in connection with hearing aids, a number of allegations having been made that these appliances were being sold at excessive prices. I believe we can assist consumers by advising them how to avoid areas of exploitation and by seeking, upon
October 20, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs our own authority and that of the provinces, to limit the extent of the exploitation. We shall consider what further powers may be necessary in order that the new department may become a vehicle for planning new legislation and developing better ways and means of providing for the protection of the consumer. We want facts before action. Before we put words on to the books of the House of Commons we want to know what the facts are and whether the proposals made will work. The enabling legislation before the house at the moment gives me and the government scope within which to move. We need a structure and organization capable of conducting a thorough investigation of new requirements and planning for the future. I expect to be back in this chamber on more than one occasion seeking approval for measures which will benefit the consumer, but I cannot and will not do this before I find out what the most effective solutions are likely to be.
The economic council has, for example, referred to the department the question of deceptive trade practices, with the suggestion that legislation might be needed to deal with them. This question has already been placed in the hands of an interdepartmental committee under the chairmanship of the deputy minister, and when the findings of the committee are available we shall take whatever action is indicated.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We will also be working on ways to improve the measurement and analysis of consumer prices and we will be working with the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to try to develop more sophisticated statistics for the use of government, and clearer methods of presenting these to the Canadian people. The economic council has stressed the need to have price statistics and information that can be translated into meaningful terms for the consumer for use in planning his or her purchases.
These, sir, are examples of the ways the new department is prepared to deal with those aspects of the question of prices which fall within our powers and responsibilities under this statute, and which fall within the constitutional limits of the federal authority. This is a first step. It is a beginning in what is going to be a very complicated process, but the establishment of this new department is not the only step.
Given the time and the co-operation of this house-and I have said every member of parliament is an advocate for the

consumer-if the house believes that I will merit its support, we will be able to make a contribution and provide assistance in the total involvement of this government on the problem of prices. But let us not fall into the serious mistake, a mistake certain members of the opposition have made, either deliberately or because they have not taken in the full scope of the bill, of assuming that prices are the only consumer problem. I was grateful to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for pointing that out in her speech this afternoon.
Of course prices are important. Of course they are foremost in the minds of the consumers, but they are not the only concern of the consumers. In passing may I say I rather doubt the accuracy of the percentages quoted in the Gallup poll because these things depend on how a question is asked. We are talking in this bill about dealing with issues relating to quality, standards, measures, safety and a host of special problems which inhibit and limit the full exercise of consumer opportunity.
We will want to look at the problem of inflammable fabrics, safety measures, the quality of children's clothing, the special needs of those who suffer from allergies, misleading packaging and excessive credit practices. These are bread and butter issues. But they are issues which the opposition, in their haste to find fault with the government, ignored in the full range of consumer interest. I refer hon. members to the resolutions passed by the Consumer Association of Canada relating to false advertising, poisoning from children's drugs, food grades and standards of labelling on food containers, frozen foods, canned juices, inflammable fabrics and a host of other commodities.
There is a wide range of issues concerning the Canadian consumer and it is the intention of this new department to deal with as many of them as is humanly possible. Finally let me say that this new department dealing with the consumer-and this is something I said when I opened the debate-will have no magical, instant solutions and panaceas. It will not offer any panacea such as the opposition suggested I should be able or prepared to do. It cannot do this because there is nothing simple or easy about the economy we live in or the issues we face.
I would be doing a disservice to this house, and through it to the people of Canada, if I were to promise pie in the sky solutions, easy
Oclober 20. 1967	COMMONS DEBATES	3351
as this would be to do. But I can promise that the efforts of this new department will be devoted toward the interests of the Canadian consumer, just as the interest of the entire government is based on finding practical workable solutions to the general problem of the cost of living. I believe the establishment of this department is a positive step on behalf of the consumers of this nation, and on this basis I ask the support of hon. members for it.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) says that the details of the bill are well known. I trust that he, as a well known labour man, will support the principle and details of this bill.
In this centennial year there have been a great many speeches in which the speakers have been looking back over the last 100 years. It also has been a popular theme to look forward into the next 100 years. I have read with interest some of the speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and other cabinet ministers. I read with interest one made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) some time ago. Most of those who forecast the future see tremendous improvements taking place. One of the areas in which improvement has been forecast is with respect to the amount of time that people will have to spend at work earning their income. We all agree that there will be, in the future, much more free time than we now have.
October 20, 1967

Canada Labour (Standards) Code Amendment
It seems to me that the time to extend the periods of holidays and other provisions for our workers is not when we get around to our second centennial but right now. It is in this vein that I bring to the house once again this bill which would amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code with regard to the provision for annual holidays with pay. At the present time the Canada Labour (Standards) Code provides an annual holiday of two weeks with pay to every employee who has been with the same employer for at least one full year. I need not go into the history of the legislation now in effect, the number of years it took to get it started, or the provisions of the first bill that was passed. The point I wish to make now is that it seems to me the time has come to start improving on this provision.
This bill proposes that the law remain as it is with respect to those who have worked for only one year for the same employer, but that in the case of those who have been with the same employer for three years or more, their annual holidays should be three weeks with pay. That is all there is to the bill. I am sure no one really is opposed to it. I am sure also that the only improvement anyone would like to make to the bill would be to extend the holidays still further after five years of employment. But surely, in 1967, no one is opposed to the idea of workers, after having worked for three years with the same employer, having three weeks annual holidays with pay.
I trust, therefore, that the house will give second reading to this bill this afternoon.

In considering any amendments to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code account must be taken of what should be done to establish minimum statutory standards, and what are the conditions which should be left to the process of free collective bargaining. The best judges of how the total wage package should be distributed in terms of benefits should be the trade union organizers, the members of the union and the union economists. They are the best judges of the necessity for wage increases, paid holidays, an increased number of statutory holidays, a better health or pension plan or other benefits for which to fight and bargain. This is undoubtedly the best system, and we as legislators and parliamentarians should establish by way of our minimum labour standards legislation decent working conditions. We should then allow the other benefits and conditions to be determined through the process of free collective bargaining, in which we all believe.
Statistics will indicate that in many cases, through the process of collective bargaining, unions have chosen to seek benefits other than the three weeks paid vacations. The headline of an article on page 4 is, "Increase in Interest Rates Impedes Housing Starts". For the moment let us consider this contention. The increased interest rate, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has argued, will not impede housing starts but will bring in more money for housing. The argument will not be answered for some months, not until we see how many houses have been started by next spring.
The article goes on to advise the membership of the union to write "to your M.L.A. or M.P." to demand that the interest rate be lowered and that the 11 per cent sales tax be removed. These people have all the answers when it comes to governmental affairs. Yet, in large black letters on a dark background of the same newspaper, we find this announcement:
Remember the 71 hour day started October 1, 1967.
Regular hours:
Days: 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
With half-hour lunch (12 noon to 12:30 p.m.
A longer lunch period is allowed in camps)
2nd and 3rd shifts:
Each work 61 hours.
Wages:
-$4.14-$4.69.
This is the sort of thing to which I object. It is time that those in all elements of the economy faced the facts of life. Profits are one thing, and the cost of lots is another. Profit may enter into the cost of lots, but included in that cost is also the matter of putting in hydro lines, underground telephone lines, and so on. Many elements enter into the high cost of living and of

Canada Labour (Standards) Code Amendment housing, and it is unfair to blame one segment of our society for these rising costs. Let us be prepared to face the economic facts of life and to do something about these costs. We need higher productivity. There is no question in my mind that wages and costs are not really important if, in our society, each head of his household receives a fair share of the gross national product, related to the amount of effort that he expends.
